01: The Homestead Act takes effect, offering settlers 160 acres of public land if they live on it and farm it. Daniel Freeman is credited with the first claim.
Flag day on the ARPANET: TCP/IP replaces the older Network Control Protocol as the network's standard.
02: President Nixon signs the Emergency Highway Energy Conservation Act, setting a national speed limit of 55 miles per hour.
03: Apple Computer, Inc. is incorporated, nine months after Steve Jobs, Steve Wozniak and Ronald Wayne started the company as a partnership.
04: NASA's rover Spirit lands in Gusev crater on Mars. Planned to last 90 Martian days, it kept working for more than six years.
05: Ford announces the Five-Dollar Day: five dollars for an eight-hour shift, in place of just over two dollars for nine hours.
George Washington Carver dies at Tuskegee, Alabama. Born in Diamond, Missouri, he taught Southern farmers crop rotation and promoted peanuts and sweet potatoes in place of cotton.
06: At the Speedwell Iron Works in New Jersey, Alfred Vail and Samuel Morse send a telegraph message through two miles of wire: 'A patient waiter is no loser.'
The last spike of the Great Northern Railway is driven at Scenic, Washington. The line reached the Pacific without federal land grants.
07: Commercial telephone service opens between New York and London, carried across the Atlantic by radio. AT&T president Walter Gifford makes the first call.
08: Ground is broken at the foot of K Street in Sacramento for the Central Pacific Railroad, the western half of the first transcontinental railroad.
Herman Hollerith is granted U.S. patent 395,782 for tabulating punched cards by machine. His machines counted the 1890 census; his company later became part of IBM.
09: At Macworld, Steve Jobs introduces the iPhone: a widescreen iPod, a mobile phone and an internet device in one. It went on sale that June at $499.
10: London's Metropolitan Railway opens: the world's first underground passenger railway. Steam locomotives pull gas-lit wooden carriages, and 38,000 people ride on the first day.
Project Diana: Army Signal Corps engineers in New Jersey bounce a radio signal off the Moon and hear the echo about 2.5 seconds later.
11: Meeting in St. Louis, a state convention votes 60 to 4 to abolish slavery in Missouri, eleven months before the 13th Amendment was ratified.
Amelia Earhart leaves Honolulu in her Lockheed Vega bound for Oakland, California: the first solo flight from Hawaii to the mainland.
12: The Schoolhouse Blizzard strikes the Great Plains after a mild morning, catching children in one-room schools. An estimated 235 people died.
13: Lee de Forest broadcasts Enrico Caruso from New York's Metropolitan Opera. Little of the singing came through, but it is regarded as the birth of public radio broadcasting.
14: The Casablanca Conference opens in Morocco. Roosevelt reached it in a Boeing 314 flying boat, the first aircraft to carry a sitting U.S. president.
15: The Pennsylvania Railroad's Federal, its brakes cut off, runs through the end of the track at Washington Union Station. GG1 No. 4876 drops through the floor. No one is killed.
16: Soyuz 4 and Soyuz 5 make the first docking of two crewed spacecraft. Two cosmonauts spacewalk from one ship to the other.
17: At 11 a.m. the submarine USS Nautilus leaves her pier at Groton, Connecticut, and signals: 'Underway on nuclear power.'
18: Eugene Ely lands a Curtiss pusher on a wooden platform on the cruiser USS Pennsylvania: the first airplane landing on a ship. Ropes weighted with sandbags stop him.
19: Apple announces the Lisa, the first mass-market computer worked through a graphical interface and a mouse. Price: $9,995.
20: Harry Truman's inauguration is the first to be televised. About 10 million people watch.
21: The first production DeLorean is announced at the factory in Dunmurry, Northern Ireland: unpainted stainless-steel body, gull-wing doors. About 9,000 were built.
22: At Spearfish, South Dakota, a chinook wind lifts the temperature from -4 F to 45 F in two minutes, still a world record. Later that morning it fell 58 degrees in 27 minutes.
Apple's '1984' commercial, directed by Ridley Scott, airs during Super Bowl XVIII to announce the Macintosh.
23: After a collision off Nantucket, wireless operator Jack Binns of the liner Republic sends the distress call CQD. About 1,500 people are saved: the first major sea rescue made possible by radio.
Jacques Piccard and Navy Lt. Don Walsh ride the bathyscaphe Trieste to the floor of the Challenger Deep, nearly seven miles down. The descent takes almost five hours.
24: Apple introduces the Macintosh: 128K of memory, a 9-inch screen and a mouse. Price: $2,495.
25: Alexander Graham Bell in New York calls Thomas Watson in San Francisco to open transcontinental telephone service.
26: McDonnell Aircraft of St. Louis flies its XFD-1 Phantom for the first time, with only one of its two engines fitted. It became the first pure jet to land on a U.S. aircraft carrier.
The Great Blizzard of 1978 crosses the Ohio Valley and Great Lakes with gusts to 111 mph. The barometer at Mount Clemens, Michigan, falls to 28.23 inches.
27: Fire sweeps the Apollo 1 cabin during a launch rehearsal at Cape Kennedy, killing astronauts Gus Grissom, Ed White and Roger Chaffee.
28: The first revenue train runs the full length of the Panama Railroad, about 48 miles from the Atlantic to the Pacific.
Space Shuttle Challenger breaks apart 73 seconds after liftoff on a freezing Florida morning. All seven crew members are lost.
29: Karl Benz applies for German patent 37435 on his three-wheeled Motorwagen with a one-cylinder gasoline engine.
30: U.S. Army Rangers, Alamo Scouts and Filipino guerrillas raid the Cabanatuan prison camp, 30 miles behind Japanese lines, and bring out more than 500 prisoners.
31: At 10:48 p.m. Eastern, Explorer 1 lifts off from Cape Canaveral: the first U.S. satellite. Its Geiger counter led to the discovery of the Van Allen radiation belt.
A blizzard that began the evening before leaves 13.9 inches of snow at St. Louis and more than 20 nearby, with five hours of thundersnow at Lambert Field.
